claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and maintenance of an adaptive dual-layer surface film.
A thin, continuous, chemically enriched oxide or hydroxide layer rapidly forms or reforms where wear disrupts the surface.
The inner oxide or hydroxide layer confers corrosion resistance.
An outer mechanically compliant layer enriched in corrosion-resistant elements such as Cr or Mo provides local wear resistance.
Continuous removal and regrowth of the dual layer reduces overall degradation relative to a material lacking dynamic film-forming capacity.
The proposed starting alloy has a near-homogeneous equiaxed microstructure and contains elements capable of forming stable protective oxides under ambient conditions.
The alloy should be tested under simultaneous sliding wear and exposure to a chloride-containing electrolyte.
The proposed structural mediator is an inner adherent passivating layer enriched in corrosion-resistant elements and an outer strain-adaptive layer that reforms after disruption.
The alloy's chemical complexity promotes segregation of elements that preferentially form protective oxides when wear exposes fresh material.
Sliding abrasion intermittently removes the surface film.
The alloy's composition and stable microstructure favor rapid re-oxidation and re-establishment of the protective barrier.

The balance between mechanical film removal and passivating-film reformation causes combined degradation to be lower than the sum of degradation measured in separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
Relative to the proposed baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have lower total material loss under identical tribocorrosion conditions.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have a lower wear-scar depth.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have a lower corrosion or passive current density.
The mechanism should operate when oxygen is available and the electrolyte is moderately aggressive, such as a neutral chloride solution.
The mechanism may fail at extremely high mechanical loads or sliding speeds because wear can outpace film formation.
The mechanism may fail in extremely acidic or alkaline media that disrupt film formation or cause uncontrolled film dissolution.
The hypothesis is rejected if combined degradation is not below the additive expectation from wear-only and corrosion-only tests or if no persistent adaptive dual-layer film is detected.
